cards.text: Pull up a stool, friend, because this is the account of Isaac, Abraham's son. At forty years old, Isaac marries Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean. FORTY! That man took his sweet time, and honestly? I respect a slow bake.
Later there's a heartache in that house, because Rebekah is barren. So Isaac does the right thing and takes it straight to the LORD in prayer for his wife.

cards.question: Isaac prays to the LORD for Rebekah because she can't have children. How does the LORD answer?

answers.text: He tells Isaac to keep waiting
He sends an angel with a sign

cards.text: But the children inside her struggle with each other, and Rebekah says, “Why is this happening to me?” Friend, they haven't even been BORN yet and they're already fighting over the armrest.

cards.question: Rebekah's children are struggling inside her, and she wants answers. What does she do?

answers.text: She goes to inquire of the LORD
She asks Isaac to pray again
She goes back to her family

cards.question: Rebekah goes to the LORD, and He answers her. What does He say is in her womb?
The LORD also tells Rebekah that one people will be stronger than the other, and the younger will serve the older.

cards.text: When her time comes, sure enough, it's TWINS! The first one comes out red, covered with hair like a fur coat, so they name him Esau, a baby who showed up already dressed for winter.

cards.question: Right after Esau comes his twin brother. How does the second twin come out?

cards.text: So the heel-grabber gets named Jacob, and Isaac is sixty years old when the twins are born. Married at forty, twins at sixty: that's TWENTY years, friend, and I used to complain about a twelve-minute oven timer.
The boys grow up, and these two may share a birthday, but they do NOT share a personality. Same oven, same batch, two completely different cookies.

cards.question: Esau, the red and hairy twin, grows up. What kind of man does he become?
Esau's twin, Jacob, grows up to be a quiet man who stays at home.

cards.text: Now, Isaac has a taste for wild game. And in this family, that's about to matter.

cards.question: Isaac has a taste for wild game, so Isaac loved ___, but Rebekah loved ___.

cards.text: One day Jacob's cooking some stew when Esau comes in from the field famished. And I mean FAMISHED, like me at three in the afternoon on a day I skipped the cookie dough.
Esau says to Jacob, “Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.” I bet he never even asked what was in it. He just saw RED.

cards.question: Because of that red stew, Esau ends up with another name. What is it?
Esau is famished and asking Jacob for stew. What does Jacob want from Esau first?
Jacob wants Esau's birthright before he hands over any stew. What does Esau say back?

answers.text: He's about to die so what good is it
Their father will never allow it
He'll just buy it back tomorrow

cards.question: Esau's ready to give up his birthright for the stew. What does Jacob make him do first?

cards.text: So Jacob gives Esau some bread and lentil stew, and Esau eats and drinks, then gets up and goes away. Friend, I've seen people think harder about a parking spot.

cards.question: Esau traded his birthright for a meal, ate it and walked away. How does the passage sum it up? Thus Esau ___ his birthright.

cards.text: And that's where we'll set this batch down for now. Two brothers, one birthright, and trust me, friend, this story's still in the oven.

findings.problem: The opening card has five sentences: 'Pull up a stool…', 'At forty years old…', 'FORTY!', 'That man took his sweet time, and honestly?' and 'I respect a slow bake.' That is over the limit of 3.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences.

findings.problem: 'That man took his sweet time' says Isaac chose to delay marrying. Genesis 25:20 gives only his age. It never says why he married at forty. The joke also makes Isaac's age the punchline.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: 'There's a heartache in that house' states a feeling as fact. Genesis 25:21 says only that Rebekah was barren and Isaac prayed. The line isn't marked as Papa Dorin's own guess.

rule.text: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: Card 4 already says 'the children inside her,' so there is more than one child. That rules out the wrong answer 'A great prophet,' which is a single person. It is also a different kind of thing from the other two answers.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'A baby who showed up already dressed for winter' makes Esau's hairy body the punchline. That is a joke about appearance.

rule.text: Never puts down any person or group: no jokes about age, gender, race, nationality, accents, appearance, intelligence or church denomination.

findings.problem: Two of the wrong words could be argued as right. 'Isaac loved Abraham' is his own father, and Abraham appears in this passage (Gen 25:19). 'Rebekah loved Laban' is her brother (Gen 25:20).

rule.text: If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The question's own setup, 'traded his birthright for a meal, ate it and walked away,' makes both wrong answers impossible. Esau can't have 'treasured' or 'protected' a birthright he just traded for a meal. That leaves only 'despised.'

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The 'story isn't over' line copies the doc's example almost word for word: 'And that's where we'll … for now … trust me, friend, this story's …'. It is not a line of its own.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
